questions.enonce_markdown: Which of the following is Oppositional inference?
questions.corrige_markdown:
Immediate inferences fall into two families. *Opposition* compares two propositions with the same subject and predicate that differ in quantity, in quality or in both. The traditional square of opposition has four relations: **contradiction** (A-O, E-I), **contrariety** (A-E), **subcontrariety** (I-O) and **subalternation** (A-I, E-O).

*Eduction* (the other family) derives a new proposition from one proposition by changing its form: **conversion** (swap subject and predicate), **obversion** (change quality and negate the predicate), **contraposition** (swap and negate both terms) and **inversion**.

Only contrariety belongs to opposition. B, C and D are eductions.

**Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Identify the form of Eduction in which given (S is P) the derived becomes (non-P is non-S):
questions.corrige_markdown:
Take the proposition "All S are P".

- **Conversion** swaps the terms: "Some P are S".
- **Obversion** changes the quality and replaces the predicate by its complement: "No S are non-P".
- **Contraposition** replaces the subject by the complement of the predicate and the predicate by the complement of the subject: "All non-P are non-S".
- **Inversion** keeps the subject and negates it with a change of quality: "Some non-S are not P".

The derived form "non-P is non-S" is therefore contraposition (it can be obtained by obverting, converting and obverting again).

**Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
Which Fallacy is most clearly committed in the following argument,

*All teachers are politicians,*
*All politicians are rebels.*
*Therefore, all rebels are teachers?*
questions.corrige_markdown:
Name the terms. The conclusion "All rebels are teachers" has **rebels** as minor term S and **teachers** as major term P; the middle term M is **politicians**. The premises are "All P are M" and "All M are S" (mood AAA, figure 4).

Check the distribution of terms:

- Middle term M: predicate of the first premise (undistributed) but subject of the second premise (distributed). It is distributed once, so there is no undistributed middle.
- Major term P: predicate of the conclusion (undistributed in an A proposition), so there is no illicit major.
- Minor term S: it is the subject of the conclusion "All S are P" and so is **distributed there**, but in the premise "All M are S" it is the predicate of an A proposition and is **undistributed**. The argument says more about S in the conclusion than the premises allow: **illicit process of the minor term**.

(A check on all subsets of a small universe, run with Python, confirms that the form is invalid.) Both premises are affirmative, so excluded premises cannot apply.

**Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
Identify the Fallacy in the following syllogism:

*All neutrons are atomic sub-particles*
*All neutrons are protons*
*Therefore all protons are atomic sub-particles.*
questions.corrige_markdown:
Name the terms: minor term S = **protons**, major term P = **atomic sub-particles**, middle term M = **neutrons**. The premises are "All M are P" and "All M are S" and the conclusion is "All S are P" (mood AAA, figure 3).

- The middle term M is the subject of both premises, so it is distributed: no undistributed middle.
- The major term P is the predicate of the conclusion (undistributed), so there is no illicit major.
- The minor term S is distributed in the conclusion (subject of an A proposition) but undistributed in the premise "All M are S" (predicate of an A proposition). This is an **illicit process of the minor term**.
- Both premises are affirmative, so the premises are not exclusive.

The only valid conclusion from these premises is the particular "Some protons are atomic sub-particles". A check with sets (Python) confirms that the universal conclusion does not follow.

**Answer: A.**

choix.texte: Illicit process of the minor term.
Illicit process of the major term.

questions.enonce_markdown:
Identify the Fallacy most clearly committed in the following argument.

*Adamu is an excellent driver because he has never had an accident.*

*Options as printed:* A) Missing the point.   B) Begging the question.   C) False clause.   D) Sequential false clause.
questions.corrige_markdown:
The argument takes the absence of accidents as the reason why Adamu is an excellent driver. An accident-free record is not a reliable sign of excellence: a person who rarely drives, or who has been lucky, also has no accident. The link between the premise and the conclusion is a **causal or evidential link that is not established**, which is the pattern of the fallacy of **false cause** (the printed option C reads "False clause", an evident misprint for "false cause").

The other labels fit less well. "Begging the question" needs a premise that already assumes the conclusion, which is not the case here. "Sequential false cause" (post hoc) infers a cause from mere succession in time. "Missing the point" (irrelevant conclusion) is also defensible, because the premise does not really support the conclusion; this is why the question is not reliable for automatic marking.

**Intended answer: C (False clause).**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.

questions.enonce_markdown: Given the premise *Either this examination is difficult or the candidates are lazy* :identify the conclusion of a valid disjunctive syllogism:
questions.corrige_markdown:
A valid disjunctive syllogism has the form $p \vee q,\ \sim p\ \therefore\ q$ (or $p \vee q,\ \sim q\ \therefore\ p$): the second premise **denies** one disjunct and the conclusion **affirms** the other. A truth-table check (Python) shows that this is valid: when $p \vee q$ is true and $p$ is false, only $q$ can be true.

Here the disjuncts are "the examination is difficult" and "the candidates are lazy". The conclusion must therefore be one of these two statements, **affirmed**:

- A and B are *denials* of a disjunct: they are the possible second premises, not conclusions.
- D is a conjunction; no valid disjunctive syllogism concludes a conjunction (both disjuncts may be true, but the syllogism does not show it).
- C affirms a disjunct. It is the conclusion obtained from the second premise "the examination is not difficult".

**Answer: C.**

choix.texte: The examination is difficult and the candidates are lazy.

questions.enonce_markdown:
Identify the order of enthymeme in the following

*All humans are fallible and all popes are human*
A Sorites is considered Aristotelian because it is in:
questions.corrige_markdown:
A sorites is a chain of syllogisms in which intermediate conclusions are left unstated. In the **Aristotelian** (progressive) sorites each premise has as subject the predicate of the one before it:

$$
\begin{array}{l}
\text{All } A \text{ are } B \\
\text{All } B \text{ are } C \\
\text{All } C \text{ are } D \\
\therefore\ \text{All } A \text{ are } D
\end{array}
$$

Unpacked, it is a series of syllogisms in the **first figure** (the middle term is subject in the major premise and predicate in the minor premise). That is why the Aristotelian sorites is said to be in Figure 1. (The Goclenian sorites reverses the order of the premises.)

**Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The procedure of the dilemma which denies the first premise is:

choix.texte: Grasping the horns of a dilemma.
Escaping between the horns of a dilemma.

questions.enonce_markdown:
The relation of the statement from $p \supset \sim q$ on the truth-table below is:

| $p$ | $q$ | $\sim q$ | $p \supset \sim q$ |
|---|---|---|---|
| T | T | F | F |
| T | F | T | T |
| F | T | F | T |
| F | F | T | T |
questions.corrige_markdown:
Recompute the last column with $p \supset \sim q$ (false only when $p$ is true and $\sim q$ is false); the Python check gives F, T, T, T, exactly as printed:

| $p$ | $q$ | $\sim q$ | $p \supset \sim q$ |
|---|---|---|---|
| T | T | F | F |
| T | F | T | T |
| F | T | F | T |
| F | F | T | T |

The column contains both T and F (one F and three T). A statement that is true under some assignments and false under others is **contingent**. It is not a tautology (always true) and not a contradiction (always false); "equivalent" describes a relation between two statements, not the status of one.

**Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The statement $(A \vee B) \equiv \sim(A \cdot \sim B)$ can be adequately applicable to which rule of inference ?
questions.corrige_markdown:
The statement has the shape of **De Morgan's theorem**: a disjunction is equivalent to the negation of a conjunction of negations, $(A \vee B) \equiv \sim(\sim A \cdot \sim B)$. (As printed, the first negation sign inside the bracket is missing; the intended law is the one just written, and a truth-table check in Python confirms it is an equivalence.)

The other rules do something else: associativity regroups three terms, commutativity swaps the order of two terms, and a tautology is a statement that is always true, not a rule that links a disjunction to a conjunction.

**Answer: B.**
themes: rules of inference and argument forms

questions.enonce_markdown: The following: *"Only women are traders"* (Wx: x is woman) ; (Tx: x is a trader) is symbolised in predicate logic as :
questions.corrige_markdown:
"Only S are P" means that nothing outside S is P, that is: **every P is S**. So "Only women are traders" says "All traders are women": for every $x$, if $x$ is a trader then $x$ is a woman.

$$
(x)(Tx \supset Wx)
$$

- A, $(x)(Wx \supset Tx)$, says "All women are traders", which is a different claim (the converse).
- B and D are existential conjunctions, "Some woman is a trader": they do not exclude male traders.

(A check with sets in Python confirms that "only women are traders" is equivalent to "the set of traders is included in the set of women".)

**Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Which of these is a religious function of myths?
questions.corrige_markdown:
Myths have several functions. Their **religious** function is to express and transmit the sacred: they tell of gods, origins and ancestors, and by doing so teach the community its religious values and beliefs and sustain its rites.

- A (norms and standards) and D (prescribing social reality) are *social or moral* functions: the myth justifies the rules and the order of society.
- C (elevating man's intellect) is closer to an *explanatory or intellectual* function.

**Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Monism is considered as a characteristic of the Pre-Socratics mainly because they:
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Monism** is the doctrine that reality derives from a **single** substance or principle. The Milesian Pre-Socratics each named one *arche* (first principle): water for Thales, the boundless (apeiron) for Anaximander, air for Anaximenes. They are monists because they reduce the variety of things to **one substance**.

B, C and D are true of the Pre-Socratics but do not define monism: rejecting myth, speculating about the cosmos and looking for the primary stuff would also be true of a pluralist such as Empedocles (four elements). Only A states the number of principles, one.

**Answer: A.**

choix.texte: Sought for the primary stuff of the universe.

questions.enonce_markdown: Which of these doctrines is attributed to Protagoras?
questions.corrige_markdown:
Protagoras, the best-known Sophist, is remembered for the **homo mensura** doctrine: "man is the measure of all things", which makes truth relative to the person judging.

- B ("Logos is a powerful master...") echoes Gorgias's *Encomium of Helen*.
- C is a conventionalist view of justice associated with sophistic thought (for example the position of Antiphon), not Protagoras's best-known doctrine.
- D is a garbled version of Gorgias's claim that nothing exists.

**Answer: A.**

choix.texte: "Man is the measure of all things..."
"Logos is a powerful master... accomplishes most divine deeds"
"Justice is a matter of not transgressing what the law prescribes"

questions.enonce_markdown: Knowledge according to Socrates is gotten by a process of rational conversation known as the:
questions.corrige_markdown:
For Socrates, knowledge is reached by **dialectic**: a rational conversation (Greek *dialegesthai*, "to converse") in which questions and answers lead the partners step by step toward a definition.

- *Elenchus* is one stage of it, the cross-examination that refutes a false opinion.
- *Maieutic* ("midwifery") describes the way Socrates helps others give birth to ideas they already carry.
- *Socratic irony* is the pretended ignorance with which he starts.

The "process of rational conversation" as a whole is dialectic. (Maieutic is also a defensible reading, so the key is open to discussion by a teacher.)

**Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: In Plato's analogy of the Divided Line, which modes of thoughts are related respectively to images and the forms?

The being of a thing according to Aristotle is?

*Options as printed:* A) Matter.   B) Form.   C) Metaphysics.   D) Substance.
questions.corrige_markdown:
For Aristotle "being" is said in several ways, but its primary sense is **substance** (*ousia*): the individual thing that exists by itself, to which the other categories (quantity, quality, place...) belong as attributes. In *Metaphysics* the substance of a thing is analysed as a union of matter and form.

- A: matter is only one element of the substance.
- C: metaphysics is the science that studies being, not the being of a thing.
- B and D are both defensible: Aristotle also says that the *form* is the essence, the "what it is", of the thing. Because two options can be defended, the question cannot be marked automatically.

The most likely intended answer is substance.

**Intended answer: D (Substance).**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.
themes: aristotle and the categories of being

questions.enonce_markdown:
For Aquinas, Faith and Reason are:

*Options as printed:* A) Mutually dependent.   B) Hierarchically dependent.   C) Mutually exclusive.   D) Independent of each other.
questions.corrige_markdown:
Aquinas holds that faith and reason **cannot contradict each other**, because both come from God: so C and D are rejected. Reason can establish the "preambles of faith" (for instance that God exists), but revelation teaches truths beyond reason (the Trinity, the Incarnation). Philosophy is therefore the servant of theology, and faith stands **above** reason, which gives a *hierarchical* relation.

Option A (mutually dependent or complementary) can also be defended as a reading of his harmony thesis, which is why this question cannot be marked automatically. The more precise answer is that they are hierarchically ordered.

**Intended answer: B (Hierarchically dependent).**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.
themes: aquinas and the nature of god

questions.enonce_markdown: According to Locke, the forms of experience are:
questions.corrige_markdown:
For Locke the mind at birth is a blank slate and **all ideas come from experience**, which takes two forms:

- **Sensation**: the external senses give us ideas of the qualities of bodies (colour, sound, hardness);
- **Reflection**: the mind observes its own operations (thinking, doubting, willing) and gets ideas of them.

"Demonstrative and intuitive" are Locke's degrees of *knowledge*, and "primary and secondary" are two kinds of *qualities* of bodies; neither names the forms of experience.

**Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The first indubitable truth discovered by Descartes' methodic doubt is:
questions.corrige_markdown:
Descartes doubts everything that can be doubted: the senses, the existence of bodies, even mathematics (the evil demon hypothesis). One truth resists, because even to doubt is to think, and to think one must exist: the **cogito**, "I think, therefore I am".

Material things (B) and God (C) are established only later, in the Meditations, after the cogito. Option A ("I am") is the existence claim contained in the cogito; the standard formulation, and the better answer, is D.

**Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Anaximenes' insight is that:
questions.corrige_markdown:
For Anaximenes the first principle (*arche*) is **air**. His insight is that a single substance can become the many things of the world by **changing its state**: air rarefied becomes fire, air condensed becomes wind, then cloud, water, earth and stone. Differences in kind are thus explained by differences in density.

Options A and B are garbled in the printed paper and do not state this idea clearly; C describes a cycle that is not the core of his teaching.

**Answer: D.**

choix.texte: Difference in the quality of our account for different kinds of things.
Difference in the quality of our account for the money existing things.

questions.enonce_markdown: With Pythagoras, number is the "Arche" because:
questions.corrige_markdown:
The Pythagoreans took **number** as the first principle: for them the things of the world are numbers, or imitate numbers, so that everything can be explained by numerical relations. The fact that "all things are made of numbers" is what makes number the *arche*, the stuff and principle of all things.

B and D (harmony from ratios, harmony in the universe) are consequences or illustrations of this idea (for instance the musical intervals), and C is a weaker version of it.

**Answer: A.**

choix.texte: All things are made of numbers.
There is harmony in the universe.

questions.enonce_markdown: Zeno's Achilles argument presupposes:
questions.corrige_markdown:
In the Achilles paradox the tortoise has a head start; whenever Achilles reaches the point where the tortoise was, it has moved on a little. Achilles must therefore cross an **infinite number of ever smaller distances**: the argument assumes that **space is infinitely divisible**. Yet the race takes place in a **limited (finite) time**, so Achilles would have to complete infinitely many steps in a finite time, which Zeno holds to be impossible.

Option A states these two presuppositions. B reverses them, and C and D claim that space and time are both infinite or both finite, which the argument does not need.

**Answer: A.**

choix.texte: An Infinite divisibility of space and limitations of time.
An Infinite divisibility of time and limitation of space.
That space and time are infinite.
That space and time are finite.

questions.enonce_markdown:
The shifting focus of the discourse of philosophy in Africa was prompted by:

*Options as printed:* A) Placide Tempels' *Bantu Philosophy*.   B) Hegel's *Philosophy of History*.   C) Paulin Houtondji's *African Philosophy, Myth or Reality*.   D) Eboussi Boulaga's *Problematique bantou*.
questions.corrige_markdown:
The debate on African philosophy passed through phases. Tempels's *Bantu Philosophy* (A) started the discussion by presenting a collective "Bantu philosophy" (ethnophilosophy). Hountondji's *African Philosophy: Myth or Reality* (C) then **shifted the focus** from the description of a collective worldview to a **critical, professional philosophy** written by individual Africans, and attacked ethnophilosophy as "myth". Eboussi Boulaga's work (D) is a critical reading of Tempels. Hegel (B) denied that Africa had a history of philosophy.

Since A can also be read as the book that "prompted" the shift, the key is not certain; the most likely intended answer is C.

**Intended answer: C (Paulin Houtondji's *African Philosophy, Myth or Reality*).**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.

questions.enonce_markdown: The thought systems of particular African communities considered as a philosophy can best be described as:
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Ethnophilosophy** is the name given (first critically, by Hountondji and others) to the collective thought systems of particular African peoples, their myths, proverbs, rites and worldview, when these are presented as a philosophy. Tempels's *Bantu Philosophy* is the usual example.

"African sagacity" refers to the wisdom of individual sages (Oruka), and "professional philosophy" to the critical, written work of trained philosophers. "African philosophy" (A) is too general: it also covers the other two.

**Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Which of Oruka's sages describes his notion of African wisdom?
questions.corrige_markdown:
Henry Odera Oruka's *sage philosophy* project distinguishes two kinds of sage: the **folk sage**, who transmits the wisdom of the community (its sayings, customs, beliefs), and the **philosophic sage**, who thinks critically and independently about that tradition. The notion of African **wisdom** (folk sagacity) is carried by the folk sage; the philosophic sage represents critical thought. "Ethnic" and "cultural" sage are not Oruka's categories.

The key is open to discussion, since "philosophic sagacity" is also his own notion of sage philosophy; the most likely intended answer is the folk sage.

**Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Which of the following is critical of the Nationalist ideological trend of African philosophy?
questions.corrige_markdown:
The nationalist-ideological trend (Nkrumah, Senghor, Nyerere...) uses philosophy to serve the **political** struggle for independence and the building of African states. Its critics reproach it for being a political programme dressed up as philosophy, that is, for its **strictly political orientation**.

B, C and D describe the aims or claims of the trend itself (valuing Africans, asserting an African philosophy, promoting liberation), not a criticism of it.

**Answer: A.**

choix.texte: It has a strictly political orientation.
It focuses in the valorisation of the Africans.
It asserts the existence of a strictly African philosophy.
It strives to promote African liberation.

questions.enonce_markdown: Which of the following pairs were proponents of Pan-Africanism?
questions.corrige_markdown:
Pan-Africanism is the movement for the unity and liberation of Africans and people of African descent. Its leading proponents include W. E. B. Du Bois (organiser of the Pan-African congresses), Marcus Garvey, George Padmore and Kwame Nkrumah.

In the options, only D pairs two Pan-Africanists. Wiredu (A, C) and Hountondji (B) are philosophers of the academic tradition, known for conceptual decolonisation and the critique of ethnophilosophy, not leaders of the Pan-African movement.

**Answer: D.**

choix.texte: Kwasi Wiredu and William Du Bois.
William Du Bois and Kwame Nkrumah.

questions.enonce_markdown:
Which Cameroonian philosopher was an ardent critic of ethno-philosophy?

*Options as printed:* A) Eboussi Boulaga.   B) Marcien Towa.   C) Njoh Mouelle.   D) Juleat Basil Fouda.
questions.corrige_markdown:
Marcien Towa (*Essai sur la problematique philosophique dans l'Afrique actuelle*) is the Cameroonian philosopher best known for his sharp attack on ethnophilosophy: for him, describing a collective worldview is not yet philosophy, and Africa needs a critical, self-affirming thought.

Fabien Eboussi Boulaga also criticised Tempels's ethnophilosophy, so option A can be defended too; Njoh Mouelle and Basil Fouda are known for other positions (the ethics of work and excellence, the philosophy of development). questions.enonce_markdown: By asserting that Africans are notoriously religious, Mbiti meant that:
questions.corrige_markdown:
John Mbiti wrote that "Africans are notoriously religious". He meant that religion **permeates every area of life**: birth, work, politics, farming, death. For the African there is no sharp line between the sacred and the secular, so the whole world view is soaked in religious thinking.

He did not claim that Africans are strictly monotheists (A) or pantheists (D); belief in a supreme being (C) is a part of the picture, but not the point of the phrase.

**Answer: B.**

choix.texte: Their world view is completely immersed in religious thinking.
They believe in the existence of the supreme being.

questions.enonce_markdown: Critics of witchcraft generally focus their arguments on the fact that:
questions.corrige_markdown:
The usual objection to belief in witchcraft is **epistemological**: the claims (that a person can harm others by occult means) cannot be tested, and no observable evidence supports them. Critics therefore stress the lack of **empirical evidence**.

The other options are weaker or secondary: the lack of "universal principles" (B) is not the classic argument, being open only to the initiated (C) describes secrecy, and the psychological explanation (D) is a hypothesis offered to account for the belief, not the main ground of the criticism.

**Answer: A.**

choix.texte: It is not based on empirical evidence.
It is not based on universal principles.
It is opened only to the initiated.
It is more psychological than real.

questions.enonce_markdown:
Which of the following is FALSE about African epistemology?

*Options as printed:* A) Specific epistemology.   B) Indigenous epistemology.   C) Social epistemology.   D) Normative epistemology.
questions.corrige_markdown:
The question asks which label is *false* of African epistemology, but it does not say what the four labels refer to, and no source is given in the paper. Discussions of African epistemology (for example Wiredu's) stress that it is **indigenous** (drawn from African languages and thought), **social** (knowledge is communal) and concerned with norms of knowing, while a claim that it is a **specific** (separate, non-universal) kind of epistemology is the one most often rejected. This points to A, but the reasoning rests on an assumed reading of the question.

For this reason the question is left open for self-assessment and no key is claimed.

questions.enonce_markdown: One of the distinguishing elements of African indigenous democracy is:
questions.corrige_markdown:
Traditional African political systems (Gyekye, Wiredu, Nyerere's "talking until agreement") rely on **consensus**: elders and councils discuss a matter until the community reaches agreement, instead of voting and letting the majority decide. "The winner takes it all" (B) is the opposite attitude, checks and balances (C) belong to the Western constitutional tradition, and "absence of political parties" (D) is a possible feature but not the distinguishing element in the usual list.

**Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: One of the main distinctions between African and Western conception of personhood is:
questions.corrige_markdown:
In the Western tradition (Descartes, Locke) the person is defined by an **individual** property such as reason or consciousness. In the African view (Mbiti: "I am because we are"; Menkiti; Gyekye) personhood is **relational**: one becomes a person through the community and through relations with others.

The options give the Western term first and the African term second ("individualistic versus relational"), so A is the intended distinction (in the opposite order to the stem). B, C and D contrast notions that are not the standard distinction.

**Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
What is the relevance of African philosophy?

*Options as printed:* A) It has rejected Eurocentrism.   B) It has led to conceptual decolonisation.   C) It has led to nationalist ideological thinking.   D) It has promoted African indigenous thinking.
questions.corrige_markdown:
The relevance of African philosophy is usually presented through Wiredu's idea of **conceptual decolonisation**: examining the concepts we use, many inherited from colonial education, and rebuilding thought from African languages and experience.

Options A (rejecting Eurocentrism) and D (promoting indigenous thinking) also describe real contributions, and C names one of its trends rather than its relevance. Since several options can be defended, the question cannot be marked automatically; the most likely intended answer is B.

**Intended answer: B (It has led to conceptual decolonisation).**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.

questions.enonce_markdown: Two determinants of a moral act are?
questions.corrige_markdown:
A human act is morally imputable only if the agent **knows** what he is doing (knowledge: the intellect understands the act and its meaning) and **wills** it (volition: the will consents freely). Without knowledge or without volition, as in an accident or an act done under constraint, there is no moral act.

Responsibility (B, C) is a *consequence* of a knowing and willing act, not a determinant of it, and "willingness and volition" (D) repeats the same element twice.

**Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: When ignorance cannot be overcome it is called?
questions.corrige_markdown:
In moral philosophy ignorance is **vincible** when the person could have removed it with reasonable effort, and **invincible** when it cannot be overcome whatever effort is made. Invincible ignorance removes responsibility, whereas vincible ignorance does not.

"Antecedent" and "consequent" describe the time of the ignorance relative to the will (before the act, or caused by the will), not whether it can be overcome.

**Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Which of these is a WEAK argument against violence?
questions.corrige_markdown:
The **slippery slope** argument claims that one violent act will inevitably lead to more and worse violence, without showing why the chain must happen. It is usually treated as a weak, often fallacious, argument.

B and C are substantive arguments against violence (social destruction, violation of the principle of the sanctity of life). D ("violence checks tyrannical systems") is actually an argument *in favour* of violence, so it is not an argument against it at all.

**Answer: A.**

choix.texte: Violence leads to destruction of the fabric of society.
Violence violates the sanity of life principles.

questions.enonce_markdown: Which of the following is a negative function of the State?
questions.corrige_markdown:
Positive functions of the State are those that serve the citizens: restraining disorder (A), defining the framework of well-being (C) and protecting liberty (D). A **negative** function is one that harms or oppresses them: demanding **obedience and unconditional subordination** (B), which turns the State into an instrument of domination.

**Answer: B.**

choix.texte: The state is a control-valve of uncontrollable action.
The state exacts obedience and unconditional subordination.
The state defines the human framework leading to human wellbeing.
The state guarantees the thriving of individual liberty.

questions.enonce_markdown: The characteristics of Aristocracy and Tyranny respectively are:
questions.corrige_markdown:
Following Plato and Aristotle, **aristocracy** is the rule of the best (*aristoi*), characterised by **excellence** (virtue) in those who govern. **Tyranny** is the corrupt form of monarchy: the rule of **one man** who governs in his own interest.

"Freedom for all" is a mark of democracy, and "wealthy few" of oligarchy; B reverses the characteristics (private interest belongs to the corrupt forms).

**Answer: C.**

choix.texte: Freedom for all and wealthy few.

questions.enonce_markdown: Codified laws governing societies adequately refers to:
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Positive law** is the law that has been *posited*, that is, enacted and written down (codified) by a human authority to govern a society, as opposed to natural law, which is not written. That is the meaning of "codified laws governing societies".

"Human law" (C) is a broader name (Aquinas's *lex humana*), "national law" (A) is only one level, and "external law" (B) is not a standard category in this context.

**Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The assertion that everything in the universe has a soul is:
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Animism** is the belief that everything in nature (people, animals, plants, rivers, rocks) has a soul or spirit.

Pantheism (C) says that everything *is* God; agnosticism (B) says that the existence of God cannot be known; deism (D) says that God created the world but does not intervene in it.

**Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The causal and design arguments for God's existence are described as:
questions.corrige_markdown:
The **causal** argument (everything has a cause, so there is a first cause) is the **cosmological** argument, and the **design** argument (the order of the universe points to a designer) is the **teleological** argument. The order matters: the question lists cause first, then design, so the answer is "Cosmological and Teleological".

D lists the right arguments in the wrong order, and the ontological argument (B, C) reasons from the very concept of God, not from cause or design.

**Answer: A.**
themes: arguments for the existence of god

questions.enonce_markdown: Moral evil is rooted in:
questions.corrige_markdown:
In the traditional answer to the problem of evil (Augustine, and the free-will defence), **moral evil** (as opposed to natural evil) comes from the misuse of **free will** by human beings: God gave humans freedom, and some choose wrongly.

God's goodness (C) and God's abandonment (D) are not causes of evil in this view, and responsibility (B) is the consequence of freedom, not its root.

**Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
Which doctrine holds that after the death of the body the soul is not certain to survive?

*Options as printed:* A) Imortality.   B) Beatific vision.   C) Transfiguration.   D) Metempsychosis.
To Peirce, the method by which thought can fix beliefs is the:
questions.corrige_markdown:
In "The Fixation of Belief" Charles S. Peirce describes four methods of fixing belief: **tenacity** (clinging to what one already believes), **authority** (letting the State or the Church decide), the **a priori** method (what seems agreeable to reason, close to metaphysics) and the **method of science**.

Only the method of science rests on an external reality that does not depend on what we think, so its results can be tested and corrected: for Peirce it is the only one by which belief can be reliably fixed.

**Answer: D.**
themes: peirce and the fixation of belief

questions.enonce_markdown: To say that 'the law is an impediment to human freedom' means:
questions.corrige_markdown:
An *impediment* is something that stands in the way. To say that the law is an impediment to freedom is to say that the law is an **obstacle** to freedom: it restricts what the individual may do. A, B and D all say the opposite, that law supports or makes possible freedom.

**Answer: C.**

choix.texte: Man is free in the presence of the law.
The law is an obstacle to human freedom.

questions.enonce_markdown:
To say that philosophy makes an inquiry into all fundamental issues and questions will most correctly mean philosophy is:

*Options as printed:* A) Analytical.   B) Critical.   C) Skeptical.   D) Rational.
questions.corrige_markdown:
Philosophy does not accept ideas as given: it **questions** the basic assumptions of every field (knowledge, morality, politics, religion) and examines them with arguments. An inquiry into all fundamental issues and questions is therefore best described as **critical**.

"Rational" (D) is also a trait of philosophy, so two options can be defended. "Analytical" (A) names one method of work (clarifying concepts), and "sceptical" (C) means doubting rather than examining. Because of the doubt between B and D, the question cannot be marked automatically; the most likely intended answer is critical.

**Intended answer: B (Critical).**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.

questions.enonce_markdown: One of the fundamental values of philosophy is that:
questions.corrige_markdown:
A classic value of philosophy is its **liberating** effect on the mind: by questioning received opinions and customs, it frees the thinker from prejudices (Russell, in the last chapter of *The Problems of Philosophy*, makes this point).

B is absurd (philosophy does not free the body), C is too narrow (it is not the main aim of philosophy), and D, a "spirit of subversion", is an accusation made against philosophers, not a value.

**Answer: A.**

choix.texte: It liberates the mind from prejudices.
It liberates the body from physical imprisonment.
It permits us to have informed religious believes.
It creates a spirit of subversion in the individual.
